overview.body:
**Samshin** (*samshin*) ​— Birth, ‌Triple Spirits ‌· Three ​spirits — ​belongs to ​the Korean ​tradition, where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Birth, ​Triple Spirits". ‌The name ​means "Three ‌spirits"[^1].

**Samshin** ​is the triple ‌spirits, often ​imagined as ​three grandmother ​goddesses, who ​govern childbirth ​and the ‌fate of newborn ​children in ‌Korean tradition. ​The name ‌means "Three ​spirits" and ‌belongs to ​the domain "Birth, ‌Triple Spirits." ​Samshin means ​"three spirits" ‌or "three ‌gods" and ‌refers to ​the deities ​who preside over ‌conception, pregnancy, ​safe delivery, ​and the ‌destiny of ​the child. ​In shamanic ‌belief the three ​spirits may ‌be distinguished ​as one ​who grants ​pregnancy, one ​who gives ‌bones, and one ‌who gives ​the soul; ‌yet they ​are also ​worshipped as ‌a single ‌goddess, Samshin ‌Halmoni.[^2]

PuniCodex restores ‌the name ​as **Samshin** ‌and serves ​its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/samshin/). The ‌restoration needs no ​distinctive letters ​or diacritics ​its ASCII ‌form would ​lose, which ​places the ​name in Tier ‌2. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *samshin* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ‌early domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).
Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985).
Lee, Jung Young, Korean Shamanistic Rituals (Mouton, 1981).

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Hangul + ​Hanja ​as **삼신 ​(三神)**. ​Etymologically ‌it means ​"Three ​spirits"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form *samshin* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ​domain-name system ​could ​not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode ‌restoration ​**Samshin** recovers ​the ‌full diacritic ‌detail ‌of the ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly in ​the ​address bar. ‌The ​restoration ​needs no ‌distinctive ​letters or ‌diacritics ​its ​ASCII form ​would ​lose, which ‌places ‌the ​name in ‌Tier ​2.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

‌- ‌**s** ‌→ **S** ​— ‌Same, capitalized
​- ​**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ​Same
- ​**m** ​→ ‌**m** — ​Same
​- **s** ​→ ‌**s** ​— Same
‌- ​**h** → ‌**h** ​— Same
‌- ‌**i** ​→ **i** ​— ​Same
- ​**n** ‌→ ‌**n** — ​Same

sources.citation: Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/sam.ʃin/** ​— Korean ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- ‌**sam** — ​The first ​syllable ‌of Samshin, ​carrying primary ‌stress in ​the ‌romanised form.
​- **ʃin** ​— The ​middle ​syllable or ​element, pronounced ‌with level ​pitch ‌in Korean.
​- **-** ‌— The ​final ‌syllable, often ​closing in ‌a nasal ​or ​simple vowel ‌in the ‌Korean ‌reading.

For ​the modern ​speaker, the ‌closest ​approximation is: ​'SAHM-sheen' — ‌The initial ​‘s’ ​is lightly ‌aspirated in ​careful speech; ‌the ​second syllable ​carries the ​Sino-Korean word ​for ‌spirit or ‌deity. The ​capital marks ‌the ​name as ​a proper ‌noun.

‌Kindred and ‌historical forms ‌of the ​name:

‌- **Hangul** ​— 삼신 ​— the ​Korean ‌script form.
​- **Hanja** ​— 三神 ​— ‌the Sino-Korean ​character form.

​The initial ​‘s’ ‌is lightly ​aspirated in ‌careful speech; ​the ‌second syllable ​carries the ‌Sino-Korean ‌word for ​spirit or ​deity. The ​capital ​marks the ‌name as ‌a proper ​noun.

sources.citation: Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in ​Hangul + ​Hanja ​as ​**삼신 (三神)** ​— ‌Korean alphabet ​+ ​Chinese ‌characters, attested ​Modern ‌Korean, ​in Korea. ‌The ​script is ​written ​left-to-right.[^1]

​The scholarly ​transliteration ‌is ​*Samshin* (Revised ‌Romanization), ​giving the ‌normalized ​reading ‌/sam.ɕin/.

The ​rendering ‌proceeds ​step by ​step:

‌- Hangul ‌삼신 ‌with ​Hanja 三神 ​— ‌the ​triple birth-fate ​deity, ‌also honored ​as ​Samsin-halmoni

‌Korean names ​may ‌be ​written in ​Hangul, ​the indigenous ​Korean ‌alphabet, ‌and sometimes ​in ‌Hanja, ​the Sino-Korean ​character ‌set. For ‌**Samshin**, ‌the ‌Hangul form ​is ‌**삼신** ​and the ​Hanja ​form is ‌**三神**. ​Hangul ​‘삼신’ and ​Hanja ‌‘三神’; ​the figure ​is ​also called ‌Samshin ​Halmoni ‌(삼신할머니). The ​ASCII ‌form ​*samshin* is ‌a ‌technological compromise; ​the ​capitalised ​restoration **Samshin** ​is ‌the ‌scholarly citation ​form.

domains.body:
**Samshin** ​is the ‌triple spirits, ‌often imagined ​as three ​grandmother goddesses, ​who ​govern childbirth ​and the ‌fate of ​newborn children ​in Korean ‌tradition. ​The name ‌means "Three ​spirits" and ‌belongs to ​the domain ​"Birth, ​Triple Spirits." ​Samshin means ​"three spirits" ‌or "three ​gods" ‌and refers ​to the ‌deities who ​preside over ‌conception, pregnancy, ​safe ‌delivery, and ​the destiny ​of the ‌child. In ‌shamanic belief ‌the ​three spirits ​may be ‌distinguished as ​one who ​grants pregnancy, ‌one ​who gives ​bones, and ‌one who ​gives the ‌soul; yet ​they ​are also ​worshipped as ​a single ‌goddess, Samshin ‌Halmoni.[^1]

### ​Three ‌Goddesses

Samshin ​appears as ​three grandmother ‌spirits who ‌together oversee ‌conception, ‌gestation, and ​birth.

### ‌Pregnancy and ​Birth

The ​spirits protect ​women ‌during pregnancy ​and ensure ​safe delivery.

​### Child's ‌Destiny

​Samshin is ​believed to ​weave or ‌decree the ​life span, ‌fortune, ​and character ‌of the ​newborn.

### ‌Household Shrine

‌A small ​domestic ​altar keeps ​the birth ​spirits present ‌and honoured ‌in family ​life.

sources.citation: Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985).
Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).

mythology.body:
The mythology ​of Samshin ‌is preserved ‌in Korean ​oral tradition, shamanic ​ritual texts, ​and classical ​sources such ​as the Samguk ‌Yusa. The ​narratives are ​not merely stories; ‌they encode ​social values, ‌ritual obligations, ​and relationships between ‌humans, nature, ​and the ​sacred. Some ​details vary by ​region and ​by shamanic ‌lineage.[^1]

### ​The Origin of ‌Samshin (Shamanic ​origin)

A ‌common shamanic ​narrative tells of ‌a girl ​or a ‌nun who ​encounters a Buddhist ​monk or ‌the Buddha ‌himself. Through a ‌series of ​trials she ​becomes the ‌mother of the ​three spirits, ​each of ‌whom receives ​dominion over a ​different aspect ‌of birth ​and fate.[^2]

‌### The Birthing ​Room Shrine ​(Household cult)

​Families placed ​a small shrine ‌to Samshin ‌Halmoni in ​the birthing ‌room or near ​the mother's ​quarters. Offerings ‌of rice, soup, ‌and clean ‌cloth were ‌made to ​thank the spirits ‌for a ​safe delivery ​and to ​ask for the ‌child's long ​life.

### ​The Gut ​for a Child ‌(Living ritual)

​When a ​child fell ​ill or a ‌woman had ​difficulty conceiving, ‌a mudang ​(shaman) would perform ‌a gut ​invoking Samshin. ‌The ritual identified ‌spiritual obstacles, ​offered petitions ​for health, ​and reconfirmed the ​bond between ‌the family ‌and the ​birth spirits.

sources.citation: Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985).
Lee, Jung Young, Korean Shamanistic Rituals (Mouton, 1981).

syncretism.body:
Samshin ​illustrates ‌the ‌deep ​interpenetration ​of ​shamanic ​and Buddhist ​idioms ‌in ​Korean ​religion. ‌The ​origin ‌myth ​often ‌involves ​a ​Buddhist ​monk, ​while ​the ‌rituals are ​performed ‌by ​mudang. ‌Confucian ​patriarchal ‌culture ​domesticated ‌the ​cult ​by ‌placing ‌it ‌under ​the ​authority of ‌the ​household, ​yet ‌the ​figure ​of ‌the ​powerful ‌grandmother ​spirit ​preserves ​an ​older, ‌female-centred theology. ‌In ​modern ‌Korea, ​Samshin ​Halmoni ‌is ‌remembered ‌in ‌childbirth ​customs, ‌fertility ​prayers, ​and ​folk ‌art, sometimes ​detached ​from ​explicit ‌shamanic ​practice.[^1]

​Within ​the ‌Korean ​tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus include ​[[baekdusan|Baekdusan]], ​[[chilsong|Chilsong]], ​[[dangun|Dangun]], ​[[halmoni|Halmoni]], ‌[[hananim|Hwanin]], ‌and ​[[hwanung|Hwanung]].

sources.citation: Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Samshin ​with certainty. ‌That ​absence ‌should ​be ​read honestly: ​for ​a ​Korean ‌name ​of this ‌type ​the ‌material ​record ‌is expected ​to ‌be ​thin, ​and ‌the ‌primary evidence ‌remains ​the ​textual ‌testimony ​gathered in ​the ‌Scholarly ​Sources ​section[^1].

‌Were such ​evidence ‌to ​surface, ​it ​would take ​recognizable ‌forms: ‌votive ​or ‌dedicatory inscriptions ​naming ​삼신 ‌(三神), ‌sanctuary ‌or ‌cult remains ​tied ‌to ​birth ​and ​iconography matching ‌its ​traditional ​attributes ​(the ‌number three ​and ​thread ​and ‌needle). ​Each candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sources.citation: Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).
